x: Corbett Tiger Reserve (India's first, Project Tiger 1973) is in Uttarakhand. Buxa is in West Bengal, Bhadra in Karnataka, and Gir (Gujarat) is a lion national park, not a tiger reserve.

Pench is the answer: the Pench forests on the Pench river straddle Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra. Kanha (MP), Manas (Assam; it adjoins Bhutan, not another State) and Sariska (Rajasthan) each lie in one State.
dispute: Most books and keys: Pench Tiger Reserve lies in two States (MP and Maharashtra). Strictly: there are two separate, adjoining tiger reserves named Pench, one in MP and one in Maharashtra, listed separately by NTCA (Shankar Environment 24 p.3; PMF Environment 03 p.91, joint TX2 Award 2023).

x: Pakhui Wildlife Sanctuary, also the Pakke Tiger Reserve, is in East Kameng district of Arunachal Pradesh, next to Nameri (Assam). It is not in Manipur, Meghalaya or Nagaland.

Bandipur (Karnataka), Manas (Assam) and Sunderbans (West Bengal) are tiger reserves. Bhitarkanika (Odisha) is a mangrove national park and sanctuary, not a tiger reserve; Odisha's tiger reserves are Similipal and Satkosia.
Dampa Tiger Reserve is in western Mizoram. Melghat is in Maharashtra, Buxa in West Bengal and Bhadra in Karnataka.

The printed key treats India's forest loss as a result of population growth during the demographic transition, with forest cover falling as population rises, so R explains A. ISFR data since the 1990s show forest cover rising slightly even as population grew.
source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.59-64 (ISFR series)
dispute: Most books and the printed key: (a) both true, R explains A. Strictly: India's forest cover has risen from about 19% (SFR 1999–2003) to 21.76% (ISFR 2023) while population kept growing, so R is not a general rule (ISFR; PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.59-64).

x: The wrong statement is that deodar grows in tidal forests. Deodar is a conifer of the temperate Western Himalaya, and tidal (mangrove) forests have Sundari, Rhizophora and Avicennia. Rosewood in evergreen forests, red sanders/redwood in deciduous forests and casuarina on beaches are correct.
source: NextGen Indian Geography 08 p.8-11; PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.45-53
evidence: PMF Indian Physical Geography 03 p.45-46, p.50-53

x: Rosewood, ebony and mahogany are typical trees of the tropical evergreen (rain) forests, which get more than 200 cm of rain. Deciduous forests have teak and sal, montane forests have conifers and oak, and mangroves have Sundari.

x: Litmus is a purple dye extracted from lichens (division Thallophyta) and is the commonest natural acid–base indicator. Palash ('flame of the forest') flowers give a yellow-orange dye and indigo leaves give the blue indigo dye; there is no litmus plant.
source: OnlyIAS NCERT Science & Tech 07 (Litmus: a natural dye)

x: Ginkgo biloba (maidenhair tree) is the classic 'living fossil': it is the only surviving member of Ginkgophyta, and its leaves are almost unchanged from Jurassic fossils. Pinus, Cedrus deodara and Ephedra are ordinary living gymnosperms.
evidence: Shankar Environment 12 (cycads also called living fossils)
